Our analysis reveals that for a fixed number of layers, increasing the width of the network generally leads to better performance, but with diminishing returns as the width increases, and that a certain width exists at which the speed of training starts to improve linearly with additional layers.  Our results were confirmed through experiments with real-world data, and further experiments showed that our findings are robust to the use of non-linear activation functions and other network architectures.  We've also explored the impact of the network size and layer number on the loss function and found that our findings to be consistent with expectations from the field.  We've also compared the performance of shallow and wide networks to other network architectures and found that our findings to be consistent with expectations from the field.

This study examines the low-temperature synthesis of bismuth ferrite (BiFeO3) nanoparticles with improved magnetic and photocatalytic properties. A comparative analysis of nanoparticles prepared using citrate-assisted pyrolysis (CAP) and a modified coprecipitation method (MC) is presented. The results show that MC nanoparticles exhibit superior magnetic properties, enhanced superparamagnetic properties, and increased thermal stability. Additionally, the MC nanoparticles display superior photocatalytic activity in terms of degradation and hydrogen production, outperforming the CAP synthesis method. This is attributed to the morphology, crystal structure, and band gap of the MC nanoparticles, which facilitate the transfer of electrons and holes in the material. The MC synthesis method offers a promising approach for creating high-performance BiFeO3 nanoparticles with improved magnetic and photocatalytic properties.

Using a simplified model based on a single family from an extended version of the standard model called SU(6), the masses of two sets of quarks are found to be related to lepton masses. In this model, the relationships between the masses of quarks, including the bottom quark, tau lepton, tau, and muon, are derived and matched with experimental results. The model's predictions for the bottom quark mass were found to be consistent with current experimental data at a 1% precision. The model's constraints were also used to make an estimate for the masses of two other families of quarks, including the top related and beauty related quarks. In this model, the masses of the top related quark were found to be significantly higher than the experimental results, indicating that the model may offer an alternative to some existing theories that have been developed to explain the masses of two sets of quarks.

Our approach enables the three-dimensional reconstruction of various objects
held by a person from a single hand view image. This is achieved through a
novel method that first estimates the shape of the hand, then generates an ideal
object shape based on the situation and uses constraints to align the object
within its optimal pose. Once the initial object shape has been estimated, we
refine it through image-based rendering and optimize the object model using
machine learning. The results are further enhanced through additional optimization
and a post-processing technique to improve the visual quality. This method can
be adapted to other applications, such as predicting object poses in images,
or to generate realistic virtual environments with accurate object
interactions.

The Ca-K index, a crucial solar parameter, is evaluated by examining the equal contrast images captured by the Schatzky-Chastain coronograph at the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory. The authors examine the variations in this index and relevant solar characteristics over the past 100 years. This index has been calculated for the period of 1929-1950 and 1997-2016 using images from the past century. Notably, a decrease in the Ca-K index was observed during the solar minimum of 1964, while an increase was seen during the solar maximum of 1981, and during the solar minimum of 2008 and subsequent maxima. This study reveals a significant increase in the Ca-K index during the solar maximum of 1981-1984, while during the solar minimum of 1964, the flux was approximately one-third of that observed in 1984. This study's findings are corroborated by the solar sunspot area, which shows a positive correlation with the Ca-K index.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at a 13 TeV centre-of-mass energy has yielded 1.0 fb of integrated luminosity. Following filtering for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ candidates, the distribution of dimuon invariant mass is analyzed. It reveals a statistically significant peak above the background level with a significance of $5.5\sigma$. The measured branching ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay is found to be $(6.58 \pm 1.58 \pm 0.20 \pm 0.24) ten to the power of -6$.

Symbolic execution, a technique for ensuring software correctness, is often hindered by its inability to handle large, concurrent programs due to test coverage constraints. As a result, significant areas of the program's execution are overlooked during symbolic execution. This work presents a solution to improve coverage under test depth limitations by introducing distributed symbolic execution, an approach that effectively addresses the scalability problem plaguing symbolic execution, thereby facilitating the examination of a broader range of program paths. To validate the effectiveness of distributed symbolic execution, this research provides a comprehensive comparison with the existing method, involving a series of experiments conducted on 12 benchmarks in both symbolic and actual execution settings, as well as a thorough discussion on the distributed approach's underlying design and performance optimization strategies.

The magnetic properties of self-assembled magnetic particle systems are examined through the perspective of the particle ensemble's magnetization relaxation behavior. An analytical model is developed to predict the time-dependent magnetization following a sudden change in the magnetic field, which is resolved analytically in the specific context of dipole-interacting particles arranged in a cubic lattice structure. Calculations for the second-order magnetic susceptibility reveal that the time-dependent relaxation process is influenced by both the applied magnetic field orientation and the arrangement of the particles. Anisotropic relaxation behavior arises due to both the inherent magnetic anisotropy in each particle and the magnetic interactions between them, leading to a complex magnetization pattern that is not strictly governed by the direction of the ensemble's magnetization.

In the context of social networks, federated learning can be a promising method to preserve user data confidentiality with a low computational burden. Federated learning enables users to collaborate on model development without needing to share their data, as the training process is distributed. While some federated learning methods utilize a central server to manage training, recent studies have shown that a central server may compromise users' data security. This paper proposes a central-server-free federated learning approach that does not require a central server to facilitate training over social networks with a single-point connection. Initially, the authors demonstrate that this method satisfies specific fairness requirements and present an efficient training algorithm that achieves this method. Furthermore, the authors conduct experiments using real-world data to validate the proposed training algorithm's effectiveness in terms of accuracy and fairness.

Recent neural network-based approaches have excelled in predictive tasks involving short texts, such as advertising click prediction and product categorization. In these tasks, data items are represented as separate vectors using specialized vectors. A sequence of data vectors is then processed by a neural network to generate predictions. Our method leverages recurrent neural networks to model temporal dependencies within a sequence and convolutional networks to capture broader patterns. This results in improved performance over current state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and training efficiency. Our model's efficacy is validated through significant 10% accuracy enhancements on the Google Log Microbenchmark and a large, private clicklog dataset (Lmc).

We have derived an analytical description of the performance characteristics at visible wavelengths for etalons that are near-perfectly in line with the optical axis, a type of configuration that is often employed in spectrographic instruments. This formulation, based on series expansion, has been refined using a combination of mathematical and numerical techniques. It allows for a detailed examination of how the etalon affects the observed spectrum, taking into account factors like its reflectivity, thickness, and optical properties. By comparing our analytical approach with results generated through simulations, we have found that the agreement is excellent. This analytical framework enables us to gain a deeper understanding of the relationships between the design parameters of the etalon and its performance, and it also facilitates the creation of more advanced etalons.

A compatible matching in a bipartite graph consists of two matchings in each set of separate parts and a perfect matching of connections between these parts, such that the individual matchings are stable and the inter-part connections are compatible within each set. We've found that in a square grid graph, if there's a large number of compatible matchings, then these matchings must be uniform and uniform, fine, and of fixed size across all parts. This result helps us develop an efficient algorithm that can identify whether a bipartite graph contains multiple compatible matchings of a certain size, by reducing it to solving the perfect matching problem.

As the integration of complex systems into smaller, specialized components continues to advance, a new trend is emerging in the form of modular components called "chiplets." By applying the principles of "accelerator engineering" to replicate custom designs from software to hardware, chiplets can be connected in unique configurations to form complete systems. This concept is similar to cluster computing, where code segments are distributed across multiple processing units to optimize performance. In response to the growing diversity of hardware, a new model called the "codelet model" is being proposed, where code segments are defined for specific hardware components. This model enables a crucial balance between programming simplicity and the customization of hardware for optimal performance.

A proposed mixture cure model allows for a more flexible estimation of the underlying distribution of observations. This method incorporates a parametric model for the observed cases and a parametric model for the incidence rate. However, a parametric assumption about the latent status distribution is required, often leading to unreliable estimates when this assumption is violated. A novel semiparametric approach is introduced, avoiding the need to specify a parametric model for the latent status distribution. The new method is applicable to various scenarios and can be adapted to situations involving right-censored data. An efficient estimation technique is implemented using a two-stage approach, combining local weighting and penalization. A comprehensive simulation study validates the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph, defined as the smallest set of vertices whose unique positions, as determined by a nonlocal distance function, allows the unique location of every other vertex to be calculated. A lower bound on the nonlocal metric dimension of a specific type of graph is established, and specific types of graphs are found where this bound equals its maximum possible value, which is two or less, depending on the graph's characteristics. Additionally, this research leads to the understanding that certain graph properties can be identified through the characteristics of a graph's order, which is related to the dimension of a graph.

In-memory computing (IMC) systems, built on emerging memory technologies, offer rapid and low-energy processing capabilities, making them suitable for high-speed applications like high-performance computing and cloud services. This paper presents an in-depth examination of the security of IMC architectures against side-channel data leaks. By using a novel attack method, we demonstrate the vulnerability of IMC systems, particularly those based on 3D Xpoint technology, to security breaches. The proposed attack is further scalable to other IMC systems and 3D stacked memory systems, and its effectiveness is shown through experiments on a 3D stacked MRAM system. To counter the attack, we suggest several robustness strategies for IMC systems, and we suggest that manufacturers release open data to mitigate the attack and ensure security.

A key technique for precisely measuring the polarization of celestial objects is the polarization modulating observatory, which uses a precise rotation mechanism to analyze the light. However, the mechanism's inaccuracy causes errors that affect the scientific results. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed an advanced method called the polarization kernel, which takes into account the device's imperfect rotation and estimates its impact on measurements. Built upon an optimization technique, the polarization kernel provides a comprehensive model of the device's behavior, but its extensive calculations make it challenging to implement in real-time for data analysis. To address this issue, we have developed a more efficient approach that uses mathematical optimization to produce a condensed, user-friendly polarization kernel that significantly reduces computational time by up to several orders of magnitude, thus enabling faster data analysis and faster scientific discovery.

Seismic data contamination by artificial sources at shallow depths causes significant interpretation difficulties. Seismic data purification, specifically removing artificial sources at known depths, is feasible through blind-spot denoising. Our proposed method involves a two-part process where the original seismic data are transformed into a new space using a learned transformation matrix, and a self-supervised model is applied to remove unwanted signals. This transformation matrix is designed using a pre-trained autoencoder, while the self-supervised model is trained and applied simultaneously. Our method's effectiveness is confirmed by applying it to a synthetic dataset.

Our research into elastic lepton-proton and antilepton-proton scattering, involving real photon production, has led us to derive advanced cross-section formulas that account for charge asymmetry. These calculations are significantly simplified, utilizing a framework based on helicity amplitudes, and are free from helicity flips, resulting in only four essential amplitudes per type of scattering. We demonstrate the application of our method with an example case of electron-positron scattering off protons, already applicable to other lepton species and neutral currents, and we discuss the potential for further analysis. We also explore the possibility of experimental validation at the MUSE facility, as well as its implications for the design of future electron-ion colliders.

The study of d$^5$ Mott insulators with strong spin-orbit coupling is of great interest due to the predicted emergence of a low-energy spin-orbit fluctuation excitation continuum that can be modeled as a spin-polaron lattice. This low-energy continuum is characterized by spin-polaron "hole" and "electron" excitations, which reorganize into a spin-polaron ladder structure when the Mott insulator is coupled with a superconducting phase. In this study, we employed scanning tunneling spectroscopy to investigate the electronic structure of the spin-orbit insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_{4}$. Our results reveal a spin-polaron ladder spectrum within the superconductor Sr$_2$Ir$_{1-x}$Mg$_x$O$_{4}$, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. The observed spectrum can be decomposed into a ladder of even-even states and odd states, with the even-odd states forming a "runway" configuration. The properties of the spin-polaron ladder spectrum provide a basis for understanding the mechanism of superconductivity in this system, with the observed results consistent with a spin-polaron-mediated s-wave superconductivity model.

A significant focus in causal analysis lies in mediation, specifically identifying how a treatment affects an outcome not only directly but also through intermediaries, leading to the definition of direct and indirect effects. This has become a crucial area in the social and biomedical sciences. However, dealing with a treatment that is not binary presents a major challenge for researchers. This problem is addressed in a recent study by proposing a multiple robust approach to mediation analysis with continuous treatments. This method involves employing a novel estimator for mediation direct effects, utilizing a combination of local polynomial regression to approximate the treatment's effect and accounting for unobserved confounding factors through an instrumental variable estimation. This enables the identification of direct effects even in scenarios with unobserved confounding factors. This method also maintains its reliability in scenarios with both unidentified and known mediating and main effects. Furthermore, it is shown to be robust against a range of misspecifications, specifically model selection and validation issues. This method is also shown to be resilient to various types of model misspecifications, specifically local misspecification of the treatment's effect and non- or non-col-linearity of the mediator with the treatment. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the proposed estimator achieves asymptotic normality and a certain level of efficiency. This is further enhanced by a Monte Carlo simulation and an application to a real-world dataset.

This special issue focuses on recent breakthroughs in the design, analysis, and implementation of starshades – devices used to block the light from a star so that an observer can examine the brightness and spectrum of other stars while keeping the star itself hidden from view. Such technologies have the potential to significantly enhance the capabilities of space-based telescopes, enabling them to analyze the light from distant stars in a way that wouldn't be possible using conventional telescopes. The issue also explores the uses of starshades in the search for life beyond Earth. A concise introduction to the issue will be followed by in-depth technical examinations of starshades made from various materials, including images of the Moon taken using different starshades. Furthermore, this issue will examine the possibilities and challenges of using starshades in the analysis of near-infrared light, with an accompanying discussion on the prospects of detecting exoplanets using a particular type of starshade.

A significant public health concern, particularly among the youth, is suicidal behavior with far-reaching consequences. Accurate early detection of suicidal risk holds the key to saving countless lives, which is currently hindered by the limitations of present-day methods. The Suicidal Text Corpus (STCorpus) has been developed to overcome these challenges by providing a comprehensive dataset for machine learning. The corpus was created using the Reddit 2017 suicide posts dataset, which was transformed into 27,800 case-control pairs and subsequently labeled as positive or negative based on the presence of suicidal content. The data was then filtered to remove irrelevant information, resulting in a dataset with high relevance. The STCorpus has been evaluated and demonstrated its potential in identifying suicidal risk factors through machine learning algorithms. The dataset has been made accessible through Zenodo with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.4553601).

This research investigates the characteristics of super Schwaartian mechanics by employing the Lagrangian approach based on the d'Hoker-Ghoussaini-Zamora model for superstring theory in AdS$_5\times S^5$, and we demonstrate that it corresponds to a specific class of sigma models within the AdS/CFT context.

The article discusses the findings on solutions for a difference equation $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$ with $0<\alpha\leq2$, focusing on how these outcomes can be applied in medical fields. Previous results by the authors on bounded solutions were improved upon, leading to a more in-depth analysis. By employing the inequality $(x+y)^2 \geq xy \geq\frac{3}{4}x^2$ and specific properties of the exponential function, novel results on bounded solutions were developed, including estimates for the upper and lower bounds. These results were applied to a model describing the dynamics of tumor growth, demonstrating the potential of using difference equations to model real-world phenomena in medicine.

We have developed a new model of electrodynamics that shares similarities with the Born-Infeld framework, addressing its limitations in describing classical phenomena. The novel model exhibits a variety of features, including finite, short-range, and angle-dependent self-interactions, and it reduces to the Born-Infeld model under specific conditions. By examining a fundamental charge model, we derived an expression for the Lagrangian and demonstrated that it can be applied to describe charged Born-Infeld black holes as a particular case. We then explored the thermodynamic properties of these black holes under different model regimes, showing that they satisfy the first law of thermodynamics. Under certain conditions, the models can also reproduce the properties of black holes in the Proca and Maxwell frameworks.

Consider a linear function $\varphi$ from a discrete group $G$ to $\mathbb{R}$. A subset $A$ of $G$ is called a $\varphi$-Sidon set if, for any subset $B$ of $G$, the set formed by the function's values at $A$ plus the function's values at $A$ repeated in $A$ (with certain repetitions ignored) has a maximum size of $|B|$. This article establishes an upper limit on the size of a $\varphi$-Sidon set when $\varphi$ has a specific form and, under certain conditions, this limit is nearly achieved. These results generalize prior findings and outcomes are achieved by employing an inequality related to the size of certain matrices and by adapting an existing proof method.

We investigate the magnetic susceptibility of an XY spin chain model with anti-ferromagnetic interactions, featuring a unique feature - a single-site anisotropy that can be adjusted. The magnitude of this adjustment influences the model's behavior, with large values triggering a quantum phase transition at absolute zero. Interestingly, near this transition point, the magnetic susceptibility exhibits scaling behavior, characterized by exponents that rely on the model's parameters. Furthermore, we explore the geometric phase in the XY spin chain and discover that it contributes to the magnetic susceptibility. Our research also reveals that the magnetic susceptibility can be broken down into two components - one corresponding to the geometric phase and the other, associated with the free energy's temperature dependence.

Our computer simulations of Ising model 3D ferromagnets reveal an unexpected outcome – a ferromagnet can actually become less stable at higher temperatures. In the case of the paramagnetic state above the critical point, as temperature increases, the time it takes for the magnetization to change does not decrease in a straightforward manner. Instead, it initially declines rapidly before plateauing and even increasing at higher temperatures. Crucially, this plateau phase begins at a temperature significantly above the critical point. These results challenge conventional understanding, as they indicate that a ferromagnet can become more stable at higher temperatures. To explain this phenomenon, we propose a theory based on the presence of 'persistent nuclear spins', accounting for the observed temperature dependence and offering a plausible explanation for the unusual behavior of various 3d ferromagnets.

In one-dimensional quasicrystals with power-law hopping, pairs can achieve localization that is otherwise unattainable for single particles. This unique characteristic is linked to the unique mathematical structure of the Fourier transforms of the quasicrystal's translation matrix and its derivatives. The formation of these localized pairs is possible when their size matches a specific value tied to the unique Fourier transforms, whereas their localization is disrupted by any size deviations. Utilizing the Fibonacci quasicrystal as a representative case, our research employs both analytical and numerical methods to verify our theoretical model's accuracy. As a result, our research indicates that quasicrystals with power-law hopping may possess novel localized states that could be useful for controlling the size of particles in processes like photoionization.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing (NLP) have significantly advanced the development of task-oriented dialogue systems, particularly in English. However, research in multilingual dialogue systems has been hindered by the gap between multilingual datasets and cross-lingual evaluation methods. To bridge this knowledge gap, this research aims to fill the void by providing an exhaustive review of existing research in dialogue system natural language processing (NLG) across languages other than English. Focusing on data-driven approaches, our study covers the key aspects: data, benchmarks, and resources. It also highlights the challenges faced by data-driven systems and proposes a new multilingual task-orientation dataset based on the TedHIV19 challenge, along with a set of tasks to address the cross-lingual data gap.

The expression of alternative splicing transcripts is regulated at multiple levels, with expression levels and alternative transcripts themselves influenced by cellular processes. To explore how short-term fluctuations in environmental and cellular factors impact alternative splicing, we analyzed RNA sequencing data from a diverse range of organisms. We developed a computational method to quantify differential expression of alternative splicing transcripts and applied it to various datasets. We found that alternative splicing is generally a stable phenomenon, with only a small fraction of genes showing sensitivity to short-term changes in conditions. When regulation of alternative splicing occurs, it tends to involve specific modes of alternative splicing, with pre-mRNA processing playing a key role. Our results indicate that alternative splicing contributes to cellular responses to diverse stimuli, with different mechanisms emerging for various types of regulation.

The EU General Data Protection Regulation has prompted companies to address data
privacy within their technology systems, yet little is known about the
implementation of technical measures in large-scale corporate compliance efforts.
To fill this research gap, we conducted a qualitative study of 41 technical
experts across the United States and Europe, gathering data on the experts'
perceptions of technical measures in addressing data privacy. Our analysis of the
data revealed the experts' perceptions of the current state of technical measures
in corporate settings, highlighting key challenges hindering their effective
incorporation into technology systems, including the lack of sufficient
resources, funding, and the current state of data privacy legislation. Based on
our findings, we offer recommendations for companies looking to effectively
incorporate technical measures in their technology systems to better comply with
data privacy requirements.

Within the framework of the Glauber-Gribov formalism, we examine the origin of long-range correlations in event-by-event multiparticle systems, with a specific focus on pA collisions. We utilize the formalism to predict the behavior of azimuthal angular correlations in multiparticle production, considering both large and moderate collision centrality classes. It is demonstrated that the formalism successfully accounts for the observed positive $v_4^{(2)}$ and negative $v_2^{(2)}$ correlations in pA collisions at RHIC and LHC facilities. Additionally, we explore power-law tail analyses of the event-by-event $N_{ch}(\phi)$ distributions to understand the underlying mechanisms of these phenomena.

The formation of light nuclei in collisions can originate from two distinct processes: the collision of nucleons and the fragmentation of resonances.  The $^{3}H$, $^{3}$He, $^{3}$H$_{2}$, $^{3}$He$_{2}$, $^{4}$He, and $^{4}$He were measured in proton, anti-proton, and light-ion momentum spectra resulting from 3 GeV Au-Au collisions.  The distribution of these particles in momentum indicates that the process of nuclear coalescence is more pronounced in collisions that produce light nuclei from fragmentation than collisions that produce light nuclei from coalescence of free nucleons.  This observation is consistent with theoretical models of nucleon coalescence.

The WFIRST exoplanet explorer is expected to be capable of detecting biomarkers in the atmospheres of planets orbiting nearby stars by analyzing light passing through these atmospheres. However, natural processes and radiation from the surrounding star can distort our view, making it difficult to detect biomarkers without prior knowledge of the surrounding light. To overcome this limitation and accurately interpret the data, it's crucial to analyze the light emitted from both the planet and its star separately. Additionally, precise measurements of the surrounding light can also be used to detect signs of past or present life-based on various possible scenarios. The primary method for achieving this involves measuring the patterns of light passing through the atmosphere at different wavelengths, but this technique alone may not yield sufficient information. To overcome this limitation, multiple approaches can be used in conjunction, such as analyzing patterns of light passing through the atmosphere at different times of the planet's orbit or analyzing patterns of light passing through the atmosphere at different wavelengths. The paper outlines a method for implementing this approach using WFIRST data, where the patterns of light passing through the atmosphere at different times of the planet's orbit can be analyzed in conjunction with the patterns of light passing through the atmosphere at different wavelengths. The paper also discusses the potential of this approach to detect biomarkers in the atmospheres of planets orbiting nearby stars.

We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for circulant graphs with at least three vertices to be dispersable. Additionally, a categorization of such graphs is provided, along with proof that a particular class of dispersable graphs falls under the (2,3)-regular dispersal pattern.

This paper presents a comprehensive approach to developing higher-order methods for efficiently computing the inverse of a matrix. The proposed methods are specifically designed to leverage the capabilities of modern GPU technology. A theoretical framework is provided, detailing the conditions for achieving convergence through iterative methods. Furthermore, a new algorithm is introduced, which incorporates a GPU-centric Solomon's House method for achieving matrix inversion. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be highly scalable, with substantial GPU acceleration over traditional CPU methods. To validate the theoretical framework and algorithm, numerical experiments are performed on a range of matrices, including those generated by the MATLAB's gallus function, which simulate real-world matrix inversion applications.

This study examines the power spectrum of cosmological perturbations that occur during ultra-low-roll inflation, which features an extremely low roll, far exceeding previously studied slow-roll inflation, resulting in significant modifications to the power spectrum. Additionally, our analysis incorporates feedback effects, which enhance the curvature perturbation and lead to even more substantial modifications during ultra-low-roll inflation, which has the potential to explain the observed features in the power spectrum at intermediate scales.

We investigate a complex optimization problem, referred to as refined assortment, which focuses on selecting a subset of basic products to offer in each store to maximize overall demand capture, taking into account customer preferences for product quality. The unique aspect of this problem is the inclusion of hierarchical relationships between products, where more premium options are associated with their base models and high-end models are associated with their base models and lower-end counterparts. This creates a multi-level structure, referred to as a tree, that the seller must consider when making decisions. The challenge lies in determining the optimal subset of products to display in each store, given that the seller cannot show different trees at each store. We have developed a heuristic solution, known as the bottom-up heuristic, which has been proven to have performance guarantees. We have also shown that the problem is computationally complex, but our computational experiments have confirmed that the heuristic solution yields significant improvements over the traditional base assortment optimization approach, given the common customer preferences for high-end and premium options.

A novel statistical approach, dubbed casebase, has been developed to analyze time-to-event data, offering an alternative to traditional survival analysis methods. This approach focuses on estimating the proportion of individuals who are exposed to the outcome of interest at a given point, which aligns with the primary goal of many clinical trials and public health initiatives. We introduce a formula to calculate the standard error of the case ratio, demonstrating that the traditional log-logistic test for comparing survival distributions is a specific scenario of the case ratio analysis. We also introduce an alternative SE formula, showing that the confidence interval for the case ratio expands as time progresses. Empirical examples from diverse fields, including oncology and epidemiology, are presented to illustrate the application of casebase analysis.

Future high-precision measurements in particle physics will require advanced methods to analyze and interpret high-energy collision data, particularly in determining key physical parameters. To achieve this, precise mathematical models based on theoretical models and observations are essential, particularly in accurately calculating complex mathematical components of these formulations. This research focuses on developing efficient computational techniques to calculate these components, particularly in the context of the Standard Model and its various mathematical frameworks. We introduce a new computational tool, AMBRE, which can be applied to a broad range of mathematical integrals and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately calculating complex components of these formulations.

High-performance storage systems are being used in scientific simulations and data analysis, including applications like the Advanced Simulation and Many-Core (ASMC) toolkit, which stores data in object format for later retrieval. This paper compares two high-performance storage systems, DAOS and Lustre, evaluating their performance on an object data storage model, also examining the object data model's performance sensitivity to system factors like multi-threading, data placement, and cache efficiency. The research reveals that both storage systems deliver exceptional performance, with DAOS surpassing Lustre in object storage efficiency and particularly excelling in areas like small object placement and single-threaded operations. The object data storage model's performance is heavily influenced by factors like data placement and cache efficiency, thereby offering potential avenues for further optimization.

The growing number of electric vehicles on the roads has led to the creation of dedicated infrastructure to facilitate rapid charging. Nevertheless, managing the capacity of these charging stations effectively is crucial to prevent long wait times for those needing a swift charge. In this paper, we present an algorithm for online admission control designed to address the challenges of electric vehicle charging stations. The algorithm aims to strike a balance between minimizing delays at the station and ensuring that only vehicles in critical need of prompt charging are allowed access. Notably, we propose a unique variant of the generalized CDS-PT policy, which has the potential to outperform existing methods while maintaining low storage requirements for policy information, making it more efficient and easier to implement.

We prove the existence of Euclidean and Hermitian linear complementary dual (LCD) codes with different parameters within finite fields. Furthermore, we present explicit constructions for Euclidean and Hermitian LCD codes with varying parameters, encompassing all possible dualities, by implementing Euclidean and Hermitian equivalence under sigma and omega transformations.

We demonstrate that classical general relativity can be reconstructed from loop amplitudes, utilizing the framework of background field theory. We establish that classical on-shell actions corresponding to tree-level loops in curved spacetime with arbitrary matter content are invariant under general relativity field transformations. This enables us to define a curved background field and confirm that the quantum effective action behaves as a local volume action, which effectively generates the off-shell classical action through the process of double copy inversion.

A widespread shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources is anticipated in the future. To determine the most cost-effective solution for reducing carbon emissions from the power sector, our study employed spatially explicit models of land use, energy, and environmental dynamics. We developed a new approach that optimizes both the management of carbon emissions and the efficient allocation of land, considering the diverse needs of various sectors. Our analysis revealed a significant land-use challenge, as inverting the decarbonization problem became infeasible due to the scarcity of available land. In response, we introduced a general model that accounts for the limitations of renewable energy sources and land use, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the limitations imposed by natural resources. Our study focused on the western United States, but our approach can be applied to any region, enabling the efficient conversion of land for solar panel and battery storage facilities while minimizing the negative impacts on ecosystems, such as habitat loss, and the diversion of water.

Cluster randomized trials, often used in vaccine evaluations, analyze the impact of different vaccine types under various allocation groups within well-matched communities. However, measuring the performance of the full vaccine schedule in real-world settings presents significant challenges. A key alternative approach is the cross-over cluster randomized design, which enables direct comparisons of different vaccine types while minimizing the impact of unknown confounders. This design also allows for rapid assessments of the full vaccine schedule's efficacy once comparisons of the different vaccine types yield statistically significant results are confirmed. A primary goal in this type of trial is to determine the risk difference between the evaluated time frame and a reference period. Although statistical software often reports risk differences directly, it typically relies on independent sampling methods, which can be inefficient in cluster randomized trials and may lead to inaccurate confidence intervals and type I errors. This study provides a framework for adapting independent sampling methods to cross-over cluster randomized trials and presents novel estimators that account for the specific challenges in cluster sampling. These proposed estimators offer several advantages over traditional approaches, including lower variance and the ability to adjust for the sampling process while maintaining unbiased estimates and coverage accuracy. A simulation-based study compares these proposed estimators with traditional ones, revealing notable benefits in terms of reduced sample sizes, shorter timelines, and the ability to conduct pre-specified interim analyses. A case study examining the evaluation of the full schedule of the inactivated trivalent influenza vaccine also applies these methods.

The normalized Laplacian spectrum of the standard fractal M\"{o}bius octagonal network is calculated and analyzed. This network's spectral analysis is then compared to other networks, such as the Koch octagonal and Sierpinski octagonal networks, and a related model is presented. As a result of this comparison, a connection between the normalized Laplacian spectrum of the fractal M\"{o}bius octagonal network and the standard Koch octagonal network is established, and its physical implications are discussed. This analysis also leads to the discovery of a relationship between the fractal M\"{o}bius octagonal and Sierpinski octagonal networks, and its applications are explored.

Contextual linear bandits pose a classic online learning challenge with a broad range of applications in real-world scenarios. In scenarios involving distributed contextual linear bandits without a shared context, we examine a setting in which multiple agents can independently receive context information and take actions based on their own estimates of an unseen parameter. These agents can then share a limited number of feedback points with a central server. We establish a centralized learning algorithm that ensures the central server can identify the underlying parameter with a minimal number of feedback points, which is determined by the dimension of the parameter. We demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of this method through theoretical analysis and further validate its performance with numerical simulations on various scenarios.

Supervised learning techniques have shown promise in extracting clinical data from text, but their effectiveness is often hampered by a lack of sufficient training data, particularly when dealing with rare diseases like cystic fibrosis. To address this challenge, this study employs unsupervised learning to create a synthetic electronic health record for cystic fibrosis patients, using real patient records from a UK-based clinical centre as a reference. By generating virtual health records, this research aims to provide healthcare professionals with valuable information for treating patients with rare diseases, thereby facilitating more effective decision-making.

Decays of the $D^{0}$ meson into specific combinations of hadrons are analyzed using a large dataset collected from proton-proton collisions. The dataset's volume equals 6 inverse femtobarns and was recorded using the LHCb detector. The study focuses on the $K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ final state, with a particular emphasis on identifying the role of the $D_{s1}^+(2530)$ and $D_{s2}^*(2573)$ charmed charmed mesons. The findings confirm the presence of these mesons in this final state, which is a key observation for their decays into specific other hadrons. The study's results also provide updated information regarding the lifetimes of the $D^0$ meson and its antiparticle, as well as the mass of the $D^0$ meson.

This paper introduces Novelpy, a Python-based algorithm that calculates the
Novelty and Disruptive Potential of published scientific studies, using two
prevalent metrics in the field of innovation research. The values are derived
from the citation network and can be visualized in a scatterplot. The values
range from low (1) to high (100,000), indicating the level of novelty and
disruptive potential. The results can be represented in a line graph, bar graph,
or heatmap. The values are normalized to stay within the defined range and are
expressed in relative terms. For example, a study with a novelty rating of 70
suggests it is 70% more innovative than the average research paper.
Novelpy's algorithm is adaptable to various datasets, such as Google Scholar,
CrossRef, Pubmed, Scopus, arXiv, and OpenCites, as well as patent data from
the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) and the European Patent
Office (EPO). The package's source code, documentation, example use cases, and
installation instructions are publicly available on GitHub at
https://github.com/boettger/novelpy.

We developed a technique that allows for the real-time adjustment of laser intensity by leveraging cross-phase modulation. Our experiment involves using two lasers: a pump beam and a signal beam. The pump beam, whose intensity can be controlled in real-time, is directed into a nonlinear optical platform to induce phase fluctuations in the signal beam. Subsequently, the fluctuation pattern is converted into a variation in laser intensity by employing a spatial light modulator. Our findings demonstrate the practical application of this intensity pattern cross-phase modulation method, as we were able to independently adjust laser characteristics such as intensity, profile, and polarization using a single pump beam. Additionally, we were able to achieve real-time modulation of up to three separate regions within the signal beam.

Humanoid robots, particularly those designed for service purposes, are expected to possess human-like abilities, but their physical capabilities are currently limited, particularly when it comes to precise hand manipulation of small objects like a bow and arrow used in archery. Researchers have conducted a thorough analysis to determine the feasibility of allowing humanoid robots into the Olympic scene, focusing on the key challenge of accurately shooting a bow and arrow. While it has been proven that, in theory, a humanoid robot can mimic a bow-and-arrow motion conceptually, several issues arise when attempting to execute it in practice, including accurately tracking the arrow's trajectory and the robot's grasp on the arrow. A 3D simulation of a humanoid robot was conducted to test its physical capabilities, revealing that accurately tracking the arrow's trajectory poses a significant challenge. The simulation showed that the arrow trajectory deviates from the expected value by approximately 20 cm, primarily due to the robot's joint precision limitations, particularly in its wrist and finger joints. These findings suggest that humanoid service robots will not be permitted in the Olympic archery competition, prompting consideration of potential modifications to the robot's design to enhance its physical capabilities.

Cross-domain recommendation systems have become increasingly popular to overcome the scarcity of user-item interaction data in target domain applications. However, most existing approaches either prioritize efficiency or effectiveness in cross-domain recommendations, but rarely achieve a balance between both. This paper presents a novel, two-step approach to address this issue, referred to as Dual Metric Learning for Cross-Domain Recommendations (DMLCDR). Initially, it leverages a similarity metric learning technique to derive target and source embeddings that are optimized for direct user-item recommendation rankings in the target domain. Next, it refines these embeddings to minimize the computational cost of the recommendation model, thereby minimizing the target embedding dimensionality. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of DMLCDR on four benchmark cross-domain recommendation datasets, showcasing its superior performance and rapid training speed compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

We've investigated the expressiveness of a certain class of modal logic, specifically within distributed systems. Our findings show that in a particular fragment of this logic, commonly used in describing systems' behaviour, all essential aspects can be represented through a single, asynchronous machine. The key to our proof lies in showing that in a system with multiple levels, where communication is possible, any necessary conditions can be met. Conversely, we've proven that this class of logic is more powerful than one that only considers the present time point, by providing a negative example that cannot be replicated using a different approach.

Our study focuses on the thermal conduction in two-dimensional, infinite plasma layers, accounting for both collective and collisional diffusion processes. We've found that in 2D systems, thermal conduction occurs more efficiently compared to the 3D scenario, with the efficiency increase tied to the inverse square root of the layer's thickness. Additionally, we've derived a comprehensive equation describing the thermal conductivity across various thickness regimes. Furthermore, we've examined the impact of 2D transport coefficients on the thermal diffusion profiles within complex plasmas under both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.

We examine the possibility of representing any given data vector as a linear combination of data vectors from a given, incomplete dataset, where the available vectors might not be fully distinct. If a data vector can always be represented in this way, we refer to the dataset as universal. Initially, we will establish a straightforward method for creating any desired dataset, though it is not always universal. Subsequently, we will identify the fundamental constraints necessary for a data vector to be represented by a linear combination of data vectors from a larger dataset, subject to the constraint that not every possible coefficient can be utilized. This will involve the derivation of the general conditions for creating a universal dataset, as well as a characterization of the datasets that are inherently non-universal.

A notable concern in X-ray angiography lies within the radiation that it emits, with most methods aiming to minimize this exposure or eliminate it altogether. Our strategy diverges from these objectives, as we seek to increase the frequency of data acquisition during X-ray angiography without elevating the radiation threshold per frame. This is achieved through the implementation of a sophisticated video interpolation technique, grounded in deep learning, which leverages an enhanced resolution prior to accurately restore missing frames. As a result, the radiation limit for each frame remains unchanged, yet the overall number of frames is enhanced. Our proposed method has been successfully tested in both simulated and real-world scenarios, showcasing its capacity to enhance image quality and precision while maintaining low radiation levels, or in some instances, reducing the latter.

The proposed FCC-ee facility will offer unprecedented opportunities for new physics discovery and precise tests of theoretical predictions of Standard Model effective field theories. The facility's heavy-flavour sector is expected to yield significant breakthroughs, thanks to an exceptionally high luminosity that will enable the production and detailed examination of numerous $c$ and $b$ hadrons. The facility's capabilities for discovering and studying heavy-quark physics are outlined, with particular emphasis on the potential for measuring rare decays of the $b$-quark, low-momentum charmed mesons, and semi-leptonic $B$ decays, as well as the potential for searching for new heavy quarks and new physics in the $Z$ pole region. The facility's current status and challenges in the detection of heavy-flavour production and semileptonic decays are also discussed.

In experiments that search for dark matter using a specific reaction type, a strong signal is produced by muon and tauon dark matter candidates. However, when these candidates interact with ordinary matter, they can lead to unwanted background events that resemble the direct conversion of dark matter particles into charged leptons. As a result, experiments need to exclude certain models in order to reach their desired level of sensitivity. A recent study has reevaluated the constraints on a particular dark matter model, $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$, and found that in some cases it can be challenging to achieve a level of sensitivity equivalent to a standard experiment. The reason for this difficulty is the specific way in which the dark matter model interacts with ordinary matter. The interaction is typically described as being "leptophilic" but in some cases it can be limited by a different type of interaction, a "neutrino floor", in experiments that use a specific reaction type. The study has found that in some of these cases, the neutrino floor can be the main constraint on the model, limiting how strongly the dark matter can interact with ordinary matter.

A large number of high-speed stars traveling much faster than typical galactic escape velocity are found to be located in the galactic bulge, with some having high speeds exceeding 500 km/s. Investigating the origin of these high-speed stars involves considering two scenarios: the stars' formation within the bulge or their ejection due to gravitational forces from a nearby massive object. Researchers have already shown that gravitational influences cannot account for the high speeds of these high-speed stars; instead, the stars' formation within the bulge or capture by dark matter or dark disc particles are potential explanations. This paper introduces a new hypothesis, the ejection of high-speed stars from the galactic center by long-term gravitational influences. We developed a method to simulate the high-speed star ejection process and found that it can successfully explain the observed distribution of high-speed stars in the galactic center, with predictions for future high-speed star discoveries and the potential detection of high-speed stars in the galactic bulge.

On an auxiliary probability space, we investigate multiplicative stochastic differential equations perturbed by additive fractional Brownian motion, assuming the Hurst parameter is within a particular range. The study relies on a regularization method using a stronger version of the equations, which yields existence of weak solutions, almost surely initial values, and for sufficiently large time, both for the original and the transformed systems. The solution process for the auxiliary equations is Markov, and when time approaches infinity, both sets of equations converge to their respective long-term equilibrium solutions, thus providing a new approach to proving existence.

The authors of this paper establish that the assertion "the non-stationary ideal on $\omega_1$ has a global nullset" remains consistent with the combination of the proper forcing axiom and the existence of a $P$-point and is also consistent with the combination of the two weakest forcing axioms, namely $0^\#$_1 and $SU$.
This conclusion is based on the derived results from the authors' previous paper [18], which were obtained by employing the $\omega_1$ analogue of the Prikry forcing technique.

Recent studies demonstrate that language models can be adapted for specific tasks via fine-tuning. However, the current adaptation frameworks have several limitations, including a lack of flexibility in model design, difficulty in switching between different downstream tasks, and inefficient use of training data. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework called Adaptor, which is centered on objectives and allows for the direct design of specialized modules for specific tasks. Adaptor offers a range of capabilities, including multi-task adaptation, dynamic switching between multiple tasks, and optimized use of training data. We provide a comprehensive framework for Adaptor, including a detailed theoretical foundation, a set of essential components, and a dynamic adaptation algorithm. Experimental results using BERT-like models demonstrate that Adaptor can switch between tasks more efficiently and perform better than traditional fine-tuning methods.

This paper presents the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset (MTSDD), which is an expansive global dataset consisting of over 300,000 images containing traffic signs from 26 different countries. The dataset is structured to facilitate various applications such as traffic sign classification and detection, allowing for global analysis and comparison of results across different algorithms and feature extracts. The dataset is comprised of images captured by participants in the 2020 Cycle Track Challenge, a component of the Mapillary Open Challenges program, on Cycle Track routes worldwide.

A widely adopted technique in recommendation systems, collaborative filtering, often relies on user-item interaction data, but this information is often scarce, prompting the development of alternative methods that don't require it. Recent innovations have introduced innovative architectures and loss functions to achieve state-of-the-art performance in recommendation systems through self-supervised learning. In this research, we present a novel self-supervised CF framework, referred to as SelfCF, composed of a straightforward architecture and a novel loss function. SelfCF utilizes a graph-based approach to construct user-item connections, employing a graph convolution network to generate user and item embeddings, while self-supervised training enhances these embeddings. The SelfCF framework outperforms current benchmarks in both synthetic and real-world datasets, boasting an efficiency of under $10\%$ training time cost.

We investigate the TEVELEV degrees of projective curves in the projective spectrum associated with a graded graded ring S. This extends the concept of TEVELEV degrees, originally defined for graded rings that are graded fields, to more general graded rings. The properties of these degrees are examined in various contexts, with a specific focus on the non-negativity of degrees that occur when a graded ring is associated with a smooth projective variety. This is further applied to the study of geometric problems in birational geometry, with a notable example given in the Noether-Farber conjecture for curves in the projective spectrum of a graded ring associated with a smooth projective variety.

We introduce a novel Dirac semimetal candidate, featuring anisotropic Dirac cones at the Fermi level with linear dispersions, accompanied by parabolic dispersions in the transverse branch. The low-energy excitation is comprised of massless Fermi arcs when the energy gap is closed. A unique gapped phase emerges when the system is tuned beyond a critical gap threshold, resulting in the coexistence of trivial and massless phases. The gapped phase is characterized by mixed linear and parabolic dispersions, featuring gapped Fermi arcs and massless surface states. The gapped phase supports topological surface states with an index of 1 and exhibits mixed linear and parabolic dispersions, persisting over a range of tuning parameters. Our research provides a pathway for experimental realization of this Dirac semimetal candidate.

In the context of population dynamics, particularly for periodic linear models with slow curves, we analyzed the entry and exit patterns of stable semi-classical trajectories. Using the Poincaré map approach, we demonstrated that these curves can be closely approximated by specific piecewise-rational functions, with the accuracy determined by specific geometric estimates. Furthermore, we derived detailed arithmetic results for a two-dimensional model, revealing the representation of trajectory points before and after entry/exit epochs under the assumption of uniform spacing in initial conditions. Additionally, we derived a representation of the Poincaré map as a composition of such rational functions for a three-dimensional model, with the first term representing the first interaction between the fast and slow components.

Future decades will see the installation of third-generation gravitational wave detectors with significantly improved sensitivity compared to earlier ones. Specifically, this enhanced sensitivity will allow them to detect gravitational waves at frequencies as high as 2 kHz. As a result, they will have the capability to detect the higher-order modes of gravitational waves of the fundamental harmonic order. Taking these detection capabilities into account, we have calculated the probability of detecting the higher-order gravitational wave modes from compact binary mergers. In doing so, we have accounted for the effects of the astrophysical environment, the instruments themselves, and the detection methods employed. By considering a variety of binary systems, we have found that, even under the most optimistic assumptions about the detectors' capabilities, the detection of the fundamental harmonic will often take precedence over the detection of the higher-order modes. Nevertheless, in certain systems where the signal strength is particularly high, it will be feasible to detect the higher-order modes. In such cases, a minimum of 20-sec integration times will be required to detect the higher-order modes of the second and third orders.

A known issue with using Gaia's astrometry to determine the masses of binary stars involves the need for full orbital periods, especially when using the double linear frequency approximation. This paper investigates whether data on partial orbits can be converted, thereby expanding the application of Gaia's astrometry to binaries at all stages of their orbital evolution. This involves developing a precise method for converting limited data into reliable results, using data from extensive simulations of binaries at various stages of their evolution. The results show that accurately weighing binaries with partial orbits is achievable, provided certain data availability and duration criteria are met, thus enabling the study of previously inaccessible binary systems.

The Genetic Algorithm, a type of evolutionary optimization technique, was initially introduced by John Holland in 1977 and is based on the concept of natural selection. The Genetic Algorithm operates by generating random initial values and repeatedly applying genetic and evaluation functions until reaching the termination condition. The crossover operation in a multi-dimensional space generates new offspring by combining two parent genes, whereas the mutation process randomly alters individual gene values. While genetic algorithms are widely used, the optimal termination method is still a subject of debate. To investigate this issue, this research aims to evaluate the effectiveness of two termination methods, specifically the maximum number of generations and total fitness value, in a 0/1 Knapsack optimization problem. Using real-world data from a reputable dataset, the study found that the selection method impacts the speed of convergence, and that the total population size should be at least twice the number of items in the 0/1 Knapsack problem. The results also indicate that the mutation rate should be in the range of 2% to 8%.

This paper is focused on $L^2$ estimates for a class of three-variable convolution oscillatory integrals defined over two-dimensional Euclidean space. Both smooth and polynomial components within the phase function are considered. Key estimates include those for $x_h$ terms, which stem from a diagonal component of the phase and are closely related to \(L^2\) estimates for bilinear oscillatory integrals, as well as off-diagonal terms, which contribute to the \(x_l\) components and are analyzed using a decomposition in frequency spaces. Building upon this, we also derive $L^2$ estimates when the oscillatory integrals are integrated over shifted curves in $\mathbb{R}^2$, yielding a constant related to the length of these curves.

This study contributes the winning solution to the Impact of Hate on Society challenge at SAARAD 2.0, where we successfully placed first. Our primary objective was to accurately identify hate speech, coupled with categorizing into sub-types. To achieve this, we conducted an in-depth evaluation of various data augmentation and model optimization strategies. Ultimately, we combined the efforts of three distinct models - fine-tuned GPT2, XLM-R, and a pre-trained T5 - trained on the official dataset and additional hate speech collections from Urdu social media and literature. Our approach resulted in a 92.72% macro F1 score without using any additional data, and a 93.01% score when using augmented data. Additionally, we found that the XLM-R 'base' model achieved the highest performance.

Recent advancements in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) forces for ions heavier than hydrogen are being explored, with a focus on understanding their behavior as the ion mass increases. This investigation reveals that forces for semi-implicit Monte Carlo (SIMet Carlo) are more efficient and consistent in their performance with increasing ion mass compared to stochastic Monte Carlo (SMC). As a result, SIMet Carlo forces can handle larger systems containing heavy ions, a capability that SMC forces cannot currently utilize due to significant performance inconsistencies. This investigation also examines the implications of using a more accurate, diffusion-free QMC approximation for the Coulomb potential on the force's efficiency and mass dependence.

The 2020 US presidential election has brought about a surge of claims regarding election fraud, predominantly shared on social media despite a lack of empirical proof. As a result, misinformation has spread rapidly, fueling an intense debate. To address this issue, our study collected and analyzed multi-modal data (images and videos, as well as text) related to election fraud from Twitter, focusing on claims of fraud in four specific areas: voting systems, voting practices, voting procedures, and voting results. Our dataset, known as VoterFraud2020, consists of 1,5,123 claims of alleged election fraud, along with 11,375 images and 1,361 videos. Furthermore, we assessed the veracity of these claims based on fact-checking information, finding that only 1.5% were verified to be true. Interestingly, the claims of voting results being falsified had the highest risk of being false, whereas those related to voting systems were the most often verified. Additionally, our study revealed that claims of alleged election fraud were often linked to fake news on fact-checking websites. To enable researchers to study the complex issue of election misinformation, we are providing VoterFraud2020 as a dataset to be used for further analysis.

We examine the development of global attractors and hyperbolicity in diffeomorphisms with positive Lyapunov exponents, and we demonstrate that in the presence of a H\"older continuous potential, the global attractor is composed of a set with a topological entropy matching the potential. This result enables us to conclude that in the case of a potential with minimal regularity, the global attractor exhibits the minimum possible topological entropy, equalling the sum of positive Lyapunov exponents, and this occurs within a context of smooth settings. Furthermore, we show the existence of a local stable manifold for points with a non-zero Lyapunov exponent in the case of a potential with minimal regularity, under the condition that the local energy decay is observed.

Deep neural networks have been enhanced with Bayesian techniques to produce predictions with a confidence measure. The methods currently in use either estimate the predictive distribution directly or generate a set of latent variables representing the posterior distribution. Our proposed approach combines the benefits of both methods by creating a compact set of variables that effectively captures the essential characteristics of the posterior distribution. The effectiveness of this approach is showcased through experiments on various regression and classification tasks, utilizing datasets with either known or unknown data distribution patterns.

One of the most effective methods to facilitate chemical reactions involves using a metal atom to bridge the gap between a low-energy state and a higher-energy state, a process that has been extensively studied in chemical reactions involving femtochemistry. In these instances, a gold atom plays a crucial role in mediating the reaction, and we examine the instanton formulation of the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory to understand how a metal atom promotes chemical reactions. The instanton method we employ is a semiclassical approximation and has notable connections to the instantons used in quantum field theory and the semiclassical tunnelling theories proposed by Levitin and colleagues. The results of our study reveal that the instanton method yields a rate constant for electron transfer that is consistent with the findings predicted by the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory. Furthermore, a comparison of the instanton method with the quantum mechanical calculations of the reaction rate reveals that the instanton method is a reliable approximation, and we also investigate the effects of external electric and magnetic fields on the reaction rate. The instanton method is also related to the quantum path integral formulation of the reaction rate, and we further investigate the quantum mechanical aspects of the reaction rate by deriving the quantum action for the reaction process. The quantum action we derive is a generalization of the instanton formulation of the reaction rate and has significant implications for the study of chemical reactions involving femtochemistry.

This research introduces a method for designing trajectory tracking control laws, which are suitable for real-world applications including those affected by external disturbances, system nonlinearities, and variable time scales. The proposed control laws are composed of two components: a foundational kinematics-based structure, which is often utilized in control systems, and an adaptive nonlinear differential equation, which allows for dynamic adjustments based on the evolving system state. This hybrid approach is capable of accommodating various inputs, constraints, and requirements, such as those related to actuator saturation, state feedback limitations, persistent disturbances, and end-point conditions.

A novel theory of the long-standing large thermoelectric effect has been developed, which is influenced by the drag mechanism involving spin fluctuations, or magnons, within a ferromagnetic material. This magnon drag effect is capable of generating the giant thermoelectric effect, which is consistent with recent experimental findings in thin-film Heusler alloys. Notably, we discovered that the thermoelectric conversion efficiency is directly related to the number of magnons involved, which depends on the properties of the magnon band, such as its width and mass. Furthermore, we found that the efficiency is maximized when the total magnetic field is reduced, which is a unique characteristic of the magnon-related giant thermoelectric effect. This novel theory provides a deeper understanding of the long-standing large thermoelectric effect, as well as the development of the magnon-based thermoelectric devices.

The problem of reaching a combined value from a set of numbers has been extensively researched in code creation and combinatorics. Notably, it's a long-standing problem in the field of combinatorics, initially proposed by Dirichlet in 1839. Dirichlet's contribution was a theoretical proof that showed the existence of a set of numbers such that any given sum of a selection from the set results in a prime number. Dirichlet's breakthrough established a vast array of possibilities in achieving perfect sums. Our study aims to reframe Dirichlet's solution as a probability problem, thereby opening doors to the possibility of applying our findings to the creation of error-correcting codes.

Let $F_q$ denote a field of $q$ elements where $q$ is non-primorial and $F_n$ denotes an irreducible polynomial of $F_q[x]$ with a degree of $n$. We will analyze the properties of $n$th powers within $F_n^m$ and utilize them to determine the higher-order elements when $m$ is between $1$ and $n-1$. This analysis will also help us understand how the minimal polynomials of these higher-order elements relate to the irreducible polynomial $F_n[x]$.

In this work, we delve into analyzing source code by converting local variables into signals and applying UPPAAL's capabilities, ultimately examining the algorithmic code from the GNU C Library for instances of dead code, unresolved dependencies, and undefined variables.

Our research introduces an innovative, end-to-end approach to optimizing metasurfaces for imaging applications. This method leverages the unique properties of the electromagnetic response at each unit cell to create diverse, spatially separate signals across the metasurface, enabling more reliable imaging results. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to collect data from metasurfaces of any size and shape, allowing us to reduce the data required for reconstruction by using a compressed sensing algorithm. We validate the performance of our method by applying it to various real-world scenarios, including imaging of multiple objects with or without a known object layout.

The interaction between an electron and a two-color, counter-rotating circularly polarized laser field gives rise to a unique spectral structure. By analyzing the energy spectrum using the length gauge, we found that the ac-Stark-shifted resonances play a significant role. We investigated how changes in the parameters of the two laser fields, including their frequencies and amplitudes, affect the visibility of these resonances in the photoionization spectrum. We discovered that when the difference between the two laser frequencies is constant, varying the amplitude of one laser field can position the ac-Stark-shifted resonances, while holding their positions steady. Additionally, we found that when the frequency ratio of the two laser fields is constant, varying the amplitude of one laser field results in a blue shift of the resonances, while the ratio of their frequencies keeps them aligned.

Deep learning-based image generation techniques have reached a high level of detail in generated images, but they fall short in accurately preserving the semantic content of original images. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative image processing method that effectively swaps the semantic content of two distinct images. This approach involves a novel transformer-based encoder that excels at capturing fine-grained semantic structures within images, as well as a custom decoder that seamlessly integrates the modified semantic structures to produce high-quality output images. Comprehensive evaluations of our approach using a range of image manipulation tasks demonstrate its capability to preserve image details and maintain the accuracy of our learned semantic content representations.

The expression of genes within a cell is a dynamic process, influenced by both the existing state of the genes and the actions of regulatory factors. This has led to the development of models based on stochastic processes, which are able to replicate the variability seen in experimental measurements of gene activity. However, analyzing these data sets to understand the underlying systems is challenging due to the limited amount of data available. This research uses a novel approach to the analysis of gene expression data that leverages the characteristics of random paths to provide new tools for understanding these systems. By employing a particular type of model, we are able to extract key pieces of information about the regulation of gene expression, including the distribution of states, the rate of transitions between states, and the impact of regulatory factors. This method is capable of handling a wide range of different models, including those that incorporate information about the past history of gene activity. This approach is demonstrated through simulations based on established models, as well as an analysis of data collected from a specific set of genes in a bacteria that had been subjected to changes in its environment.

In this approach, initial model parameters are set through an unsupervised analysis of input data, with the goal of minimizing uncertainty about the labels for each data point. This uncertainty is calculated based on how well different parameters produce the same output from a given data point. By training a classification model using the uncertainty at each data point as its target, the final model parameters can be refined. This overall framework is versatile, but in its basic form, it falls short of achieving the performance of a supervised model. To improve upon this, we suggest a two-step approach where the initial stage involves training a feature transformation along with the unsupervised stage. This feature transformation helps to increase the diversity of the feature space and makes the uncertainty more specific to the data point of interest. This results in a more accurate classification model. Furthermore, we propose a method to incorporate prior knowledge into the semi-supervised learning process, thereby enhancing its performance. This is demonstrated through a series of experiments on various datasets, including a toy dataset, MNIST, and the Street View CrowdSourcing (SVC) image dataset.

A crucial challenge in the context of Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) is how to effectively combine the application of machine learning and quantum computing principles. The quantum machine learning approach, specifically Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), and the quantum machine learning approach, specifically Quantum Neural Circuits (QNCs), are two different methods that have distinct advantages and applications. The purpose of this paper is to explore the characteristics of QNNs and QNCs using the quantum approximation optimization method (QAOA) and its layer-wise application (LQAOA). Through numerical simulations, we have discovered that the performance of LQAOA increases with its layers up to a point of stabilization, after which it does not continue to improve. This phenomenon is influenced by the choice of initial parameters and the type of problem being solved. Moreover, we have found that the training process of LQAOA is sensitive to the quality of the classical part, with deep and well-trained networks being more susceptible to flaws in the classical circuits.

The objective of person re-identification is to locate multiple images or videos of the same individual within a database containing multiple persons, given one or more known samples of the person.
